title: Verbal nouns
intro: A verbal noun turns a verb into a noun, so it can take case and possessive endings like *ev* or *kitap*. English does the same with **-ing** and **to**: *Yüzmeyi seviyorum* (I love swimming), *Gelmeni istiyorum* (I want you to come). This unit covers the infinitive `-mAk` with its case endings, `-mA` with possessive endings for an action that has its own doer, `-(y)Iş` for a single act or a way of doing something, and three ways of saying **in order to**.

sections.title: Yüzmeyi seviyorum: the infinitive as a noun

blocks.text: You know `-mAk` as the dictionary form of a verb ([A1 unit 6](gp-infinitive-stem)) and as a subject: *Burada sigara içmek yasak* ([A2 unit 6](gp-gerek-lazim)). It is a noun: *yüzmek* is **to swim** and also **swimming**. Like any noun, it takes the case its verb asks for. You say *Çayı seviyorum* (I love tea) with the accusative, so you say *Yüzmeyi seviyorum* (I love swimming).

Before a case ending that begins with a vowel, the k of `-mAk` disappears and the buffer y takes its place: *yüzmeyi*, *yüzmeye*, *okumayı*, *okumaya*. Before a consonant it stays: *yüzmekten*, *okumakla*. Many grammars describe *yüzmeyi* as the shorter verbal noun `-mA` + accusative; the forms you say are the same either way.

**No case** after *istemek*: for **to want to**, use the bare infinitive: *Gitmek istiyorum* (I want to go), *Ne yapmak istersin?* (What would you like to do?). This is the commonest verbal noun of all. *Gitmeyi istiyorum* exists, but sounds formal or insistent.
**The other verbs** take the case they take with any noun. Learn them in pairs, the way Turkish speakers feel them: *-(y)I sevmek*, *-(y)A başlamak*, *-DAn korkmak*.

blocks.text: Two verbs change their meaning with the infinitive. *Çalışmak* is **to work** or **to study**, but *-mAyA çalışmak* is **to try to**: *Uyumaya çalışıyorum* (I'm trying to sleep). And *bırakmak*, **to leave** something somewhere, becomes **to quit** a habit: *Kahve içmeyi bıraktım* (I've stopped drinking coffee).

items.en: What do you like doing in your free time?
Last year I started playing the guitar.
The child is afraid of sleeping in the dark.
In the end he decided to quit smoking.
The whole day went by in reading.
We want to move to Izmir next year.

blocks.text: French marks the same thing with little words: j'aime nager, j'ai commencé à nager, j'ai peur de nager. Its à lines up with the Turkish dative (*yüzmeye başladım*) and its de with the ablative (*yüzmekten korkuyorum*) surprisingly often.
The k of `-mAk` drops, it doesn't soften: *yüzmeyi*, never *yüzmeği*. And *-mAyA* is spelled with a y between the vowels: *başlamaya*, *okumaya*.
The locative *-mAktA* (in the act of) belongs to formal Turkish and comes in [B2 unit 5](gp-makta): *Toplantı devam etmektedir* (The meeting is in progress).

The infinitive has no subject of its own: in *Gitmek istiyorum*, the one who goes is the one who wants. When someone else does the action, Turkish uses `-mA` with a possessive ending that names the doer: *Gitmeni istiyorum* is **I want you to go**, literally **I want your going**. You met the pattern in [A2 unit 6](gp-gerek-lazim): *Gitmem lazım* (I need to go: **my going is necessary**).
Then comes the case the main verb needs, as with any possessed noun. The third person puts the n of [A1 unit 10](gp-pronominal-n) before it: *gelmesini*, *gelmesine*, *gelmelerini*.

blocks.text: **The doer** is shown by the possessive ending alone when it is a pronoun: *(senin) gelmen*. A noun goes in the genitive, like an owner ([A1 unit 10](gp-genitive)): *Ali'nin gelmesi* (Ali's coming, that Ali comes), *otobüsün gelmesi* (the bus coming).

**As a subject**, it goes with *lazım* and *gerek*, as in [A2 unit 6](gp-gerek-lazim): *Gitmemiz lazım* (We have to go); with the dative, *Gelmene gerek yok* (There's no need for you to come). [B2 unit 4](gp-clause-as-subject) takes clauses as subjects further.

**Tense** isn't marked: the main verb and the context place the action. *Gelmesine sevindim* is **I was glad he came** or **I'm glad he's coming**. The negative goes inside: *gelmemesi*, his not coming.

items.en: My mother wants me to go to bed early.
We're waiting for the bus to come.
I'm so glad you came.
We were surprised that Ali didn't come.
Her father didn't let her go.
Everyone wants her to win.
There's no need for you to come.

blocks.text: English needs a clause or an object + **to**: **I want you to come**. French needs a whole clause in the subjunctive: je veux que tu viennes. Turkish turns the action into a noun with an owner, and treats it like any other object.

blocks.title: Gelme: don't come, or coming?
blocks.text: The negative `-mA` and the verbal noun `-mA` look alike. In *Gelme!* (Don't come!) the stress falls on *GEL*; in the noun the stress falls on the suffix. With an ending there is no doubt: *gelmen* can only be **your coming**, and *gelmemen* **your not coming**.

blocks.title: Verbal nouns that became words
blocks.text: Some `-mA` nouns are everyday words now: *dondurma* (ice cream, from *dondurmak*, to freeze), *dolma* (stuffed vegetables, from *dolmak*, to fill), *buluşma* (a meeting, a date), *konuşma* (a talk, a speech).

`-(y)Iş` (four-way harmony, with the buffer y after a vowel) names one act, or the way something is done: *yürümek* → *yürüyüş* (a walk; the way someone walks), *gülmek* → *gülüş* (a laugh, a smile), *bakmak* → *bakış* (a look, a glance). With a possessive it describes a person's manner: *Gülüşü annesine benziyor* (Her laugh is like her mother's).
Many `-(y)Iş` nouns have become ordinary words, and you see them on every sign in an airport or a station.

*Gitmek* softens before the vowel, as in *gidiyor*: *gidiş*. A return ticket is *gidiş dönüş bilet*, a ticket for the going and the coming back. Sports and outings use *yürüyüş yapmak* (to go for a walk, to hike) or *yürüyüşe çıkmak* (to go out for a walk).

**`-mA` or `-(y)Iş`?** `-mA` is the general verbal noun, the one that takes a doer and fits after *istemek* or *sevinmek*. `-(y)Iş` is narrower: one act (*bir yürüyüş*, a walk), a manner (*yürüyüşü*, the way he walks), or a fixed word (*giriş*, *uçuş*). When in doubt, use `-mA` for the action and learn the `-(y)Iş` nouns as words.

items.en: Where is the entrance to the museum?
The exit door is on the left.
Our flight is at five.
A return ticket, please.
In the evenings we go for a walk by the sea.
Her laugh is like her mother's.

blocks.text: *Giriş* and *çıkış* also mean **entry** and **leaving** as events: *Giriş ücretsiz* (Admission is free), *Çıkışta ödeyin* (Pay on the way out).
Turkish has three ways to say why someone does something, from the most general to the most formal.

Where

Meaning
rows: after verbs of going and coming
He went to Germany to work.

blocks.text: **`-mAk için`** is the infinitive with the *için* (for) of [A1 unit 12](gp-icin): **for swimming**, **in order to swim**. It works with any verb: *Sınavı geçmek için çok çalışıyor* (She's studying hard to pass the exam).

**`-mAyA`** is the dative, the case of direction, after *gitmek*, *gelmek*, *çıkmak*, *koşmak* and other verbs of movement. It's the everyday way to say what you are off to do: *Ekmek almaya çıktı* (He's gone out to buy bread), *Bize yemeğe gelin* (Come to us for dinner) with a noun, *Seni görmeye geldim* (I came to see you) with a verbal noun.

**`-mAk üzere`** is the formal **in order to** of news and official letters: *Ali, çalışmak üzere Almanya'ya gitti*. You met *üzere* with personal endings in [B1 unit 2](gp-about-to), where it means **about to**: *Çıkmak üzereyim* (I'm about to leave). After a verb of going, it is purpose; as a predicate with `-(y)Im`, `-sIn`, it is **about to**.
**A different doer.** When the one who acts isn't the subject, use `-mA` with a possessive before *için*: *Herkesin duyması için yüksek sesle konuştu* (He spoke loudly so that everyone could hear).

items.en: I came to Istanbul to learn Turkish.
On Sunday we went to the sea to swim.
My mother has gone out to buy bread.
I came to see you.

items.tr: Herkesin duyması için yüksek sesle konuştu.

blocks.text: French pour + infinitive matches *-mAk için*, and aller nager or je suis venu te voir match *yüzmeye gitmek* and *seni görmeye geldim*: no word for **to**, just a verb of movement and a verb of purpose.

*-mAk için* means **in order to**, never **because**. **Because he came** needs another form, *geldiği için*, which comes in [B1 unit 8](gp-digi-icin). For now, give reasons with *çünkü* or *bu yüzden*.

summary: `-mAk` is a noun and takes the case its verb needs: *yüzmek istiyorum*, *yüzmeyi seviyorum*, *yüzmeye başladım*, *yüzmekten korkuyorum*.
Before a vowel the k drops and y appears: *yüzmeyi*, *yüzmeye*; before a consonant it stays: *yüzmekten*.
*-mAyA çalışmak* is **to try to**; *-mAyI bırakmak* is **to quit** a habit.
`-mA` + possessive gives an action its own doer: *Gelmeni istiyorum*, *Ali'nin gelmesine sevindim*; third person *gelmesini*, *gelmesine*.
`-(y)Iş` names one act or a manner, and many everyday words: *yürüyüş*, *giriş*, *çıkış*, *uçuş*, *gidiş dönüş*.
**In order to**: *-mAk için* anywhere, *-mAyA* after verbs of going and coming, *-mAk üzere* in formal Turkish; *-mAsI için* for a different doer.
